## Proof

The statement is **true**. In fact, it holds for any measure space (completeness is not needed), with injection constant $C = 1$.

**Setup.** Equip $L^1 \cap L^\infty$ with the norm $\|f\|_{L^1\cap L^\infty} := \max(\|f\|_1, \|f\|_\infty)$, which is equivalent to the sum norm. We must show that for every $p \in [1,\infty]$ there exists a constant $C_p$ such that
$$\|f\|_p \le C_p\, \|f\|_{L^1\cap L^\infty}, \qquad \forall f \in L^1\cap L^\infty.$$

**Endpoints.** For $p=1$: $\|f\|_1 \le \max(\|f\|_1,\|f\|_\infty) = \|f\|_{L^1\cap L^\infty}$. For $p=\infty$: $\|f\|_\infty \le \max(\|f\|_1,\|f\|_\infty) = \|f\|_{L^1\cap L^\infty}$. Both hold with $C=1$.

**Interior, $1 < p < \infty$.** Let $f \in L^1 \cap L^\infty$. Write $|f|^p = |f|\cdot|f|^{p-1}$. Since $|f|^{p-1} \le \|f\|_\infty^{p-1}$ a.e.,
$$\int_\Omega |f|^p\,d\mu \le \|f\|_\infty^{p-1}\int_\Omega |f|\,d\mu = \|f\|_\infty^{p-1}\,\|f\|_1.$$
Taking $p$-th roots,
$$\|f\|_p \le \|f\|_\infty^{(p-1)/p}\,\|f\|_1^{1/p}.$$
This is the standard interpolation (log-convexity) inequality $\|f\|_p \le \|f\|_1^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty^{1-1/p}$.

Now use the elementary fact $a^\alpha b^{1-\alpha} \le \max(a,b)$ for $a,b\ge 0$ and $\alpha\in[0,1]$: with $a=\|f\|_1$, $b=\|f\|_\infty$, $\alpha = 1/p$,
$$\|f\|_p \le \max(\|f\|_1,\|f\|_\infty) = \|f\|_{L^1\cap L^\infty}.$$

**Conclusion.** For every $p\in[1,\infty]$,
$$\|f\|_p \le \|f\|_{L^1\cap L^\infty}, \qquad \forall f\in L^1\cap L^\infty,$$
so the identity map $L^1(\Omega,M,\mu)\cap L^\infty(\Omega,M,\mu) \hookrightarrow L^p(\Omega,M,\mu)$ is linear and bounded (with operator norm $\le 1$), hence a continuous injection. The argument uses only the pointwise bound $|f|^{p-1}\le\|f\|_\infty^{p-1}$ and Hölder/trivial estimates, so completeness of $\mu$ plays no role; the statement holds a fortiori for complete measure spaces.

Therefore the statement is **true**.
